claims.text: The initial alloy is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a simple crystal structure.
Adding a controlled amount of carbon through powder metallurgy will improve the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi.
Adding carbon through powder metallurgy will improve the mechanical performance of CoCrFeNiTi.
Carbon modification will preserve the favorable plasticity of CoCrFeNiTi.
Carbon modification will preserve the favorable machinability of CoCrFeNiTi.
Carbon addition will produce carbide precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
The carbide precipitates will act as obstacles to dislocation movement.
Obstruction of dislocation movement by carbide precipitates will cause precipitation hardening.
Carbide precipitation hardening will enhance the alloy's hardness and mechanical performance.
Heat treatment after powder-metallurgy processing will ensure homogenization.
Heat treatment after powder-metallurgy processing will produce precipitation hardening.
The carbon-modified alloy will have at least 15% greater hardness than the unmodified alloy.
The carbon-modified alloy will have at least 10% greater yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
The carbon-modified alloy will maintain at least 5% elongation at break.
The hypothesis is intended to apply for processing temperatures from 1000 °C to 1200 °C.
The hypothesis is intended to apply for testing temperatures from 25 °C to 600 °C.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires at least a 15% hardness increase and a 10% yield-strength increase, whereas the falsification rule only requires 10% and 5%, respectively. Results between these thresholds would fail the stated prediction but would not falsify it under the stated rule.
